---
title: "Ergodicity in driven supersonic turbulence"
---

```{=html}
<script type="module" src="../app/js/widgets.js"></script>
```

Statistical turbulence theory makes statements about *ensemble averages*: the mean of a quantity over
infinitely many realisations of the flow that share the same forcing statistics. Nobody measures an
ensemble. An observer, or a simulation, has one realisation. It provides either a *time average* at
a fixed point (a probe, an anemometer, a spectrograph pointed at one line of sight) or a *volume
average* at a fixed time (a snapshot, a map). Using either in place of the ensemble assumes the flow
is ergodic. This chapter explains the assumption, shows what it rests on, and sets up a run in
which it can be tested. The laboratory panel at the end lets you do the test yourself.

## Three averages {#sec-ergo-averages}

Let $q(\mathbf x, t)$ be a field of the flow, for example the log-density $s = \ln(\rho/\rho_0)$, and
let $\omega$ label the realisation (in a simulation: the random seed of the driving). There are three
averages:

$$
\langle q\rangle_\text{ens}(\mathbf x, t) = \lim_{M\to\infty}\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M q(\mathbf x, t; \omega_m),\qquad
\overline{q}^{\,T}(\mathbf x) = \frac1T\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T} q(\mathbf x, t)\,dt,\qquad
\langle q\rangle_V(t) = \frac1V\int_V q(\mathbf x, t)\,d^3x .
$$ {#eq-averages}

The ensemble average is the object of the theory. The other two are what we can compute. Two
properties of the turbulence connect them:

- **Statistical stationarity.** If the statistics do not change in time, $\langle q\rangle_\text{ens}$
  does not depend on $t$. Driven turbulence becomes stationary after a few large-eddy turnover times,
  once the injected energy is balanced by dissipation.
- **Statistical homogeneity.** If the statistics do not change from place to place,
  $\langle q\rangle_\text{ens}$ does not depend on $\mathbf x$. A periodic box driven by a force whose
  statistics are translation invariant is homogeneous.

The ergodic hypothesis is the statement that, in a stationary flow,

$$
\lim_{T\to\infty}\overline{q}^{\,T}(\mathbf x) = \langle q\rangle_\text{ens}
$$ {#eq-ergodic}

for almost every realisation. Birkhoff's theorem [@birkhoff1931] proves this for any measure-preserving
dynamical system whose invariant measure cannot be split into two invariant parts (metric
transitivity). The theorem is exact, but its hypothesis cannot be checked directly for the Navier–Stokes or
MHD equations, let alone for their discretisations. For turbulence, ergodicity is a working
assumption. It is supported by experiments and simulations [@frisch1995; @galanti2004; @djenidi2013], not proved.
The analogous statement for volume averages, $\langle q\rangle_V \to \langle q\rangle_\text{ens}$ as
$V\to\infty$, rests on homogeneity plus the decay of spatial correlations. In a box of fixed size $L$
it is only approximate: a box holds a finite number of independent large eddies.

**What the literature shows.** The rigorous results need help from the model, namely stochastic forcing.
Hairer & Mattingly [-@hairer2006] prove that the 2-D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, driven by
white noise acting on only a few Fourier modes, have a unique invariant measure, so time averages
converge to the same limit from every initial condition. Romito [-@romito2004] proves ergodicity for a
*finite-dimensional* approximation of the 3-D equations driven by degenerate noise. We know of no
proof for the full equations with deterministic forcing, and none for compressible MHD. Our driver
(Ornstein–Uhlenbeck amplitudes on 14 modes) is of the stochastic kind these theorems assume, but our
equations are compressible, isothermal and magnetised. The theorems make the hypothesis plausible
here. They do not establish it. The direct numerical tests compare averages and find agreement: Galanti &
Tsinober [-@galanti2004] report temporal and spatial statistics of a long forced periodic-box
Navier–Stokes run to be clearly similar, which they present as evidence for ergodicity, not a proof;
Djenidi, Tardu & Antonia [-@djenidi2013] compare temporal and spatial averages in simulated grid
turbulence; Higgins et al. [-@higgins2013] find, from lidar data, that atmospheric surface-layer flows
are ergodic above uniform surfaces, away from sharp transitions. There are counter-examples. In long *ideal* (non-dissipative), Fourier-truncated MHD
runs the lowest modes keep large means compared with their fluctuations, which Shebalin
[-@shebalin2013] calls broken ergodicity. In forced, dissipative MHD, McKay et al. [-@mckay2017] found
that an ensemble of runs with identical parameters and sinusoidal forcing showed large long-time
differences in cross helicity, and question ergodicity for that forcing. MHD, our case, is where
the assumption has been seen to fail, so it is worth testing.

::: {.callout-note title="What is proved and what is assumed"}
*Proved:* Birkhoff's theorem, for measure-preserving, metrically transitive systems; a unique invariant
measure for noise-driven 2-D Navier–Stokes [@hairer2006] and for noise-driven, truncated 3-D
Navier–Stokes [@romito2004]. *Assumed:* that
a driven, dissipative turbulent flow, or its numerical model, has such an invariant measure on its
attractor and samples it. The test below is evidence for or against that assumption in one run,
not a proof.
:::

## How long is long enough? {#sec-ergo-time}

The limit $T\to\infty$ in @eq-ergodic is never reached, so the question is how fast the time average
converges. Successive values of $q$ at one point are correlated. If the normalised autocorrelation
function is

$$
C(\tau) = \frac{\langle (q(t)-\bar q)(q(t+\tau)-\bar q)\rangle}{\sigma_q^2},\qquad
\tau_\text{int} = \int_0^\infty C(\tau)\,d\tau,
$$ {#eq-acf}

then for $T \gg \tau_\text{int}$ the variance of the time average is

$$
\operatorname{Var}\big(\overline{q}^{\,T}\big) \simeq \frac{2\tau_\text{int}}{T}\,\sigma_q^2
= \frac{\sigma_q^2}{N_\text{eff}},\qquad N_\text{eff} = \frac{T}{2\tau_\text{int}} .
$$ {#eq-neff}

A record of length $T$ is worth $N_\text{eff}$ independent samples, however finely it is sampled.
Sampling every second time step, as our probe does, resolves $C(\tau)$, but more samples per
$\tau_\text{int}$ do not shrink the error bar. In practice $\tau_\text{int}$ is estimated by integrating
the measured $C(\tau)$ up to its first zero crossing. That estimate is biased low when the record is
short, which makes the error bar too small. The laboratory shows how $\tau_\text{int}$ and
$N_\text{eff}$ change as you shorten the window.

For supersonic turbulence the natural unit is the large-scale crossing time
$t_c = L/(\mathcal M c_s)$. At a fixed point, $\tau_\text{int}$ is set by how long a structure takes
to sweep past, so it is a fraction of $t_c$ for velocities, and longer for the density. A run of ten
crossing times, the conventional length of a driven-turbulence study, gives at most a few tens of
independent samples per point. Statistics measured from a single probe therefore carry error bars of
order $\sigma_q/\sqrt{N_\text{eff}}$, which can be several tenths of $\sigma_q$.

## Volume, mass and time weighting {#sec-ergo-weighting}

A probe at a fixed point weights each moment of time equally, and so samples the *volume-weighted*
distribution: a point spends a fraction of time inside dense gas equal to the volume fraction of
dense gas. It does not sample the mass-weighted distribution. For isothermal supersonic turbulence
the volume-weighted PDF of $s$ is close to a Gaussian [@vazquez1994]:

$$
p_V(s) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_s^2}}\exp\!\Big[-\frac{(s+\sigma_s^2/2)^2}{2\sigma_s^2}\Big],\qquad
\sigma_s^2 \approx \ln\!\big(1 + b^2\mathcal M^2\big),
$$ {#eq-lognormal}

with $b \approx 1/3$ for solenoidal and $b \approx 1$ for compressive driving in 3-D
[@federrath2010; @price2011]. The mean $\langle s\rangle_V = -\sigma_s^2/2$ is fixed by mass conservation,
$\langle\rho\rangle_V = \rho_0$. The mass-weighted PDF is the same Gaussian shifted to $+\sigma_s^2/2$. An
ergodicity test has to compare like with like: the probe's time PDF with the volume PDF. The rms Mach
number has the same issue. Its volume-weighted value is dominated by fast, nearly empty gas, and its
mass-weighted value by the dense gas that holds the kinetic energy (see the feedback in @sec-ergo-setup).

## Setting up a test {#sec-ergo-setup}

A test of @eq-ergodic needs a flow that is, as far as possible, stationary and homogeneous by
construction. Then any remaining difference between time and volume statistics is evidence about
ergodicity, or about the length of the run, and not a trivial consequence of the set-up.

**Driving with a finite set of modes in real space.** The acceleration is

$$
\mathbf a(\mathbf x, t) = A(t)\sum_{m} 2\,\mathrm{Re}\big[\hat{\mathbf a}_m(t)\,e^{2\pi i\,\mathbf k_m\cdot\mathbf x/L}\big],
$$ {#eq-forcing}

a sum over the 14 integer wave vectors with $1 \le |\mathbf k| \le 3$ in the plane (one of each $\pm\mathbf k$
pair). Each amplitude $\hat{\mathbf a}_m$ follows an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with correlation time
$t_c/2$ [@eswaran1988], projected onto its solenoidal part [@federrath2010]. The process is sampled
on a fixed grid of times and interpolated linearly, so $\mathbf a$ is a deterministic function of
$(\mathbf x, t)$. It is evaluated analytically in every cell of every level, at that level's own time.
That is why the force is the same on all levels. Each cell receives the *exact cell average* of
@eq-forcing (each Fourier mode times $\prod_d \operatorname{sinc}(k_d\Delta x/L)$), so the average of the
fine-level force over a coarse cell equals the coarse-level force to rounding
{{< test "driving: the same force on every level" "restriction of the fine kick" >}}. A spectral
driver that computes the force on one grid by FFT could not be applied to a nested hierarchy
this way. Since the wave vectors and the OU statistics are translation invariant, so are the
statistics of the force. That is the homogeneity needed above.

**Isothermal gas.** The total energy is reset to $\rho c_s^2/(\gamma-1) + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \tfrac12 B^2$
after every update, with $\gamma = 1.01$ in the Riemann solver, so $p = \rho c_s^2$ holds exactly in every
cell {{< test "driven run" "p = ρ cs² everywhere" >}}.

**Mach-number feedback.** After every root step, the overall amplitude $A$ is
multiplied by $(\mathcal M_\text{target}/\mathcal M)^{\Delta t/t_\text{fb}}$, with $t_\text{fb} = t_c/5$ and the
logarithm of the factor clamped to $\pm 0.25$. $\mathcal M$ is measured on the root level, which holds the
restricted fine data, so it covers the whole box. We control the **mass-weighted** rms Mach
number $(\sum\rho v^2/\sum\rho)^{1/2}/c_s$, which measures the kinetic energy. Controlling the
volume-weighted value failed in our first tests: in 2-D at Mach 10 it is dominated by evacuated
regions. An acceleration drives gas at $\rho = 10^{-4}$ exactly as hard as dense gas, so the voids reach
high speeds. Holding their Mach number at 10 throttled the driving until the dense gas had slowed to
Mach 4. Both values are recorded. The mean momentum injected by $\rho\mathbf a$ (non-zero, because
$\rho$ and $\mathbf a$ are correlated) is removed after every root step by a Galilean shift applied to
all levels.

**The probe.** The cell of the finest level whose lower corner is the box centre (one of the four most
central cells) is recorded every second step of that level: $t$, $\rho$, $\mathbf v$, $\mathbf B$, $p$ in
`Float64`. Records are buffered and appended to a binary file during the run, so a long run never holds
its whole history in memory, and a run that crashes loses only the unflushed buffer. The format is
self-describing: a magic string, the variable names, the cell position and size, and a JSON metadata
string, followed by fixed-length records. A Julia reader (`read_probe`) and the JavaScript reader of the
laboratory decode it. The test suite checks the round trip
{{< test "driven run" "probe file round trip" >}}.

**Why 2-D, and what nesting does to the test.** The run is 2-D (one cell thick in $z$, periodic) so
that ten crossing times fit in a CPU run of about an hour. 2-D turbulence differs from 3-D
turbulence: energy cascades to large scales, and coherent vortices live long. Both lengthen
correlation times. The probe sits in the finest level, which resolves the central quarter of the box
four times better than the root. Its statistics are those of the better-resolved flow. The volume
statistics are computed in two ways: over the finest level (same resolution as the probe, but only a
quarter of the box in each direction) and over the root (the whole box, at a quarter of the
resolution, holding restricted fine data in its centre). The density PDF depends on resolution in its
tails, so the two volume PDFs bracket the comparison.

## The run {#sec-ergo-run}

Root $64^2$ (periodic), two refined levels of $64^2$ cells each covering the central half of
its parent, so the finest level resolves the central quarter of the box with $\Delta x = L/256$; the
children span the box in $z$ (one root cell thick). Isothermal, $c_s = \rho_0 = 1$, uniform initial
$B_x$ with $\beta = 2p/B^2 = 200$, CT, HLL, Courant 0.4, `Float64`. Driven to $t = 1 = 10\,t_c$ with
seed 1. Script: `core/bench/run_mach10.jl`.

- **Cost.** 493 s on two CPU threads. The levels took 6 944 / 15 723 / 28 314 steps, 2.3 and 1.8 per
  parent step on average.
- **Constraint.** $\max|\nabla\cdot\mathbf B|\,\Delta x/\max|\mathbf B|$ stayed between
  $2\times10^{-15}$ and $5\times10^{-14}$ on every level (sampled every $0.01$).
- **Mach number.** The mass-weighted rms Mach number reaches 10 after about $0.3\,t_c$ and overshoots to 12 before the feedback catches it. Over
  $t \ge 3\,t_c$ it averages $10.02$ with a standard deviation of $1.50$ (range 7.5–13.4); the
  volume-weighted value averages $10.33 \pm 1.33$. The feedback holds the *mean* at the target. The 15 %
  fluctuations about it are the variability of a flow driven by 14 modes, which a controller acting
  on a time scale of $t_c/5$ does not remove (a faster one oscillated in our tests).
- **The probe.** 14 157 records (every second finest step), 1.02 MB, at
  $(x, y) = (0.50195, 0.50195)$.

**Time against volume, over $3\,t_c \le t \le 10\,t_c$:**

| | probe (time) | finest level (volume) | whole box, root (volume) |
|---|---|---|---|
| mean of $s = \ln\rho/\rho_0$ | $-2.15 \pm 0.27$ | $-1.92$ | $-1.88$ |
| variance of $s$ | $3.11$ | $3.25$ | $4.66$ |

The time mean at one point agrees with the volume mean of the finest level within 0.9 standard
errors, and the variances within 5 %. The standard error comes from @eq-neff: for $s$ the
integral time at the probe is $\tau_\text{int} = 0.081\,t_c$, so the seven crossing times hold about
$N_\text{eff} = 43$ independent samples. For $v_x$ it is $0.31\,t_c$ and $N_\text{eff} \approx 12$: the
velocity is correlated four times longer than the density, and its time mean ($-2.5 \pm 1.9$) is
correspondingly uncertain.
The ACF of $s$ does not simply decay: after its first zero at $0.25\,t_c$ it swings negative and
returns to $+0.2$ near one crossing time (open the lab to see it). Integrating only to the first zero
ignores that structure, so $N_\text{eff}$ is an estimate, good to perhaps a factor of two, not a measurement.

Read this as *consistent with* ergodicity at the level of means and variances in one run: not as a
confirmation. Three cautions:

1. **Resolution.** The whole-box variance (4.66) is larger than the finest-level one (3.25), although
   the root is coarser. The two volumes differ in more than resolution: the finest level sees only the
   central $1/16$ of the area, and over seven crossing times a region that small does not sample all
   large-scale states of the box. Which of the two the probe should agree with is part of the question.
2. **The shape of the PDF.** Neither PDF is the lognormal of @eq-lognormal. The measured mean $-1.92$
   differs from $-\sigma_s^2/2 = -1.62$ because the PDF is skewed toward low densities. With
   $\sigma_s^2 \approx 3.2$, @eq-lognormal would require $b \approx 0.48$. That number is from 2-D
   solenoidal driving, at modest resolution, and is not comparable with the 3-D values quoted above.
3. **Non-conservative safeguards.** Voids reach $\rho \sim 10^{-5}$. A density floor
   ($10^{-6}$) and the reflux guard of @sec-reflux-guard act there. Both change the low-density tail,
   which the time PDF at one point samples rarely.

The ensemble below, eight runs that differ only in the seed of the driving, gives an independent
estimate of the scatter between time averages.

### The ensemble {#sec-ergo-ensemble}

Seven more runs with identical set-up and seeds 2–8 (seed 1 is the run above) give an ensemble of
eight. Each took 8–19 minutes. Over $3\,t_c \le t \le 10\,t_c$:

| | mean over the 8 runs | scatter between runs |
|---|---|---|
| time mean of $s$ at the probe | $-1.91$ | $0.37$ |
| volume mean of $s$, finest level | $-2.03$ | $0.25$ |
| volume mean of $s$, whole box | $-1.94$ | $0.07$ |
| mass-weighted rms Mach number | $10.0$–$10.9$ per run | |

Three results:

1. **The time averages are consistent with the ensemble.** The eight probe time means scatter by
   $0.37$ about their mean. The error bar @eq-neff assigns to each one averages $0.45$, so the
   estimate is about right, if anything slightly conservative. The ensemble mean of the time means,
   $-1.91 \pm 0.13$, agrees with the whole-box volume mean, $-1.94$. In each run, the difference between
   the probe's time mean and the finest-level volume mean, in units of its error bar, lies between
   $-0.85$ and $+1.37$ (rms 0.71). This is what ergodicity predicts for means. It does not prove it.
2. **The variance is a property of the run, not of the ensemble, over seven crossing times.** The
   time variance of $s$ at the probe ranges from $3.1$ to $7.2$ between runs. Within each run it
   follows the variance of the finest level closely: the ratio is $0.91$–$1.15$, and the
   correlation over the eight runs is $0.96$. Its correlation with the whole-box variance, which
   is much steadier ($4.7$–$5.7$), is only $0.39$. One point and the region around it share the same
   history of large-scale flow, and seven crossing times are not enough for that history to
   average out. Read at face value, a single run of this length would misjudge the ensemble variance
   of $s$ by up to 40 %. That is a sampling error, not a failure of ergodicity, but it is the
   practically relevant one.
3. **An unexplained sign.** The time mean of $v_x$ at the probe, and the finest-level volume mean of
   $v_x$, are negative in all eight runs ($-0.4$ to $-3.9$), while the whole-box volume mean scatters
   around zero ($-1.2$ to $+0.8$). We tested whether the nesting causes this. A point-symmetric
   problem (2-D Orszag–Tang) keeps its symmetry to rounding on the nest
   ($|\rho - \rho_\text{rot}|/\rho \le 7\times10^{-16}$ to $t = 0.5$), as it does on a uniform grid. In
   cheaper runs (root $16^2$), the central volume mean of $v_x$ is again negative for seeds 1–8 on the
   nest. On a uniform $64^2$ grid it is negative for five of the same eight seeds, and the run-by-run
   values are not correlated with the nested ones. Seeds 9–14 on the nest give mixed signs (4 of 6
   $\ge 0$). These tests cannot tell whether this is a property of the realisations or a weak bias of the
   nested scheme under Mach-10 conditions (floors, the reflux guard), with a run-to-run scatter of
   several $c_s$. Eight negative signs in a row has a chance of 1 in 128 (two-sided). We have not found
   a cause and report it as open.


### A positivity guard for refluxing {#sec-reflux-guard}

This run found a failure of plain Berger–Colella refluxing. At $t \approx 0.063$ a nearly empty
root cell beside the level-2 footprint ($\rho \approx 5\times10^{-4}$) received the momentum
correction of its face, $\Delta(\rho v)\sim (\Delta t/\Delta x)\,\Delta(\rho v^2 + p)$ from much denser fine
gas. Divided by its tiny density, that is a velocity of hundreds of $c_s$. The new velocity entered the
child's ghost zones, the child's boundary flux grew, and so did the next correction: within
$10^{-3}$ time units the velocity reached $3000\,c_s$ and the time step $10^{-6}$. The same happened
without a magnetic field. The correction is now applied only if the corrected cell keeps a positive
density and a positive thermal energy, as in Enzo. A skipped correction breaks exact conservation in
that one cell. None of the conservative test problems trigger it: the suite still conserves to
rounding.

## Explore it {#sec-ergo-lab}

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="ergo"></div>
```

The panel reads the probe file directly, `app/data/mach10_probe.bin`, the same bytes the
simulation wrote. Move the averaging window and watch three things: the time PDF at the probe against
the volume PDFs, the autocorrelation time and the number of independent samples it implies, and the
running time average closing in on the volume average, or failing to.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Shrink the window to one crossing time and slide it along the run: the time PDF of a single point over
one $t_c$ looks nothing like the volume PDF. Then widen it to the full stationary interval.

:::
